name: Wild Mushroom Galettes
why: Mushroom season is peaking right now, and Mary Berry takes her classic garlic-mushroom vol-au-vent and turns it into six free-form galettes. Golden puff cases packed with browned wild mushrooms in a crème fraîche and Parmesan sauce — proper autumnal, and a brilliant showstopper for a light lunch or starter.
author: Henry
ingredients: 250g large flat mushrooms, cut into 8 wedges
50g Parmesan or vegetarian hard cheese, finely grated
finely chopped flat-leaf parsley, to garnish
salt and freshly ground black pepper

steps: Preheat the oven to 200C/180C fan/Gas 6 and line a baking tray with parchment paper.
On a floured work surface, roll the puff pastry into a 28x20cm rectangle about 3mm thick.
Lightly score a criss-cross pattern over the surface (do not cut through), then stamp out six rounds with an 8.5cm/3in cutter.
Chill the pastry rounds on the tray for 10 minutes, then brush the tops with the beaten egg.
Put a large roasting tin in the oven to get very hot. Add the oil, butter and garlic, then the chestnut and flat mushrooms. Season and toss.

Put the tin on the bottom of the oven and the pastry tray near the top. Bake 18-20 minutes — pastry should be well risen and lightly golden; the mushrooms should be brown with most of their juices evaporated.
Remove both trays. Slice the galettes in half widthways, peel out any uncooked pastry from the middles, and turn the tops upside down on the baking sheet.

Add the wild mushrooms and crème fraîche to the roasting tin and mix. Return both trays to the oven for 8-10 minutes until the pastry cases are crisp and the crème fraîche has turned into a mushroom-coloured sauce.
Stir the Parmesan and lemon juice into the mushroom sauce and season well.
Spoon the mushroom filling into half the pastry cases.
Garnish with chopped parsley, top with the other pastry halves and serve immediately.

pro_tips: Browning the mushrooms properly is the whole game — if the juices are still there when you plate, the filling will be soggy. A screaming-hot tin and a low oven shelf do the dehydrating work for you.
Can t find wild oyster or shiitake? Two different shop-bought varieties (chestnut + king oyster) still give you the layered texture and flavour you want.

name: Briam: Traditional Greek Roasted Vegetables
why: The classic Greek roasted-vegetable tray that's the natural side to moussaka. Thin-sliced potato, courgette and red onion layered in a pan of canned tomatoes, seasoned with oregano, rosemary and garlic, then baked until soft, charred and all the juices have reduced to a sweet, saucy glaze. Vegetarian, hands-off, and serves a crowd.
author: Mart
ingredients: 570g (1¼ lb) golden potatoes, peeled, thinly sliced into 5mm rounds
570g (1¼ lb) courgette (2–3), thinly sliced into 6mm rounds
1 large red onion (or 2 small), thinly sliced into rounds
Greek extra virgin olive oil, plus extra for serving
794g (28 oz) can diced tomatoes with juice (no-salt-added organic recommended)

steps: Preheat the oven to 200C/180 fan/gas 6 and place a rack in the middle.
Put the sliced potatoes and courgette in a large mixing bowl. Season with salt, pepper, oregano and rosemary.
Add the parsley, minced garlic and a generous drizzle of extra virgin olive oil, and toss until the vegetables are well coated.
Pour half the canned tomatoes into a large round oven-safe pan (an 11-inch/28cm pan) and spread them over the bottom.
Arrange the seasoned potatoes, courgette and sliced onion in rows around the pan, alternating the vegetables.
Pour any remaining oil and garlic mixture over the vegetables, then top with the rest of the diced tomatoes.
Tent the pan loosely with foil so it isn't touching the vegetables, and bake for 45 minutes.
Remove the foil, then roast uncovered for a further 30-40 minutes, until the vegetables are soft and charred and most of the liquid has evaporated. Ovens vary, so check as you go.
Remove from the oven and serve warm or at room temperature with a generous final drizzle of extra virgin olive oil.

pro_tips: Slice the potato thin (5mm) so it cooks through in the same time as the courgette - uneven thickness is what makes one tray of briam soggy and another undercooked.
The uncovered second half of the bake is where the flavour comes from: the tomato sauce must reduce and caramelise. If it's still swimming at the end, give it 10 more minutes.
